segments.t: What changed in the current release. The version this guide was built for is shown in the footer.

KTPH007Coding agentsKTPH008 — korTTY recognises Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI in local shell tabs and classifies each pane as working, blocked on a question, done or idle, and now shows it everywhere: a glyph in the tab title, chips, accent bars, rollups and pane rows in the dashboard (which expands to a waiting agent and offers Send Enter / Esc / Interrupt in the context menu), a dockable KTPH009Coding AgentsKTPH010 panel (KTPH011View → Coding AgentsKTPH012, KTPH013KTPH001KTPH014+KTPH015KTPH002KTPH016+KTPH017KTPH003KTPH018) listing every agent of every window with one-click answers (y, n, Enter, Esc, ↑, ↓, Ctrl+C), Explain, Rename and a prompt box, a status-bar strip, KTPH019KTPH004KTPH020+KTPH021KTPH005KTPH022+KTPH023KTPH006KTPH024 to jump to the next waiting agent, a badge with the number of waiting agents on the app icon (Dock, Windows taskbar, KDE/Ubuntu launcher; window title elsewhere) and a desktop notification when an agent needs a decision or finishes while you are not looking at its pane. Detection reads the terminal screen locally and can be switched off in KTPH025Settings → Terminal → Coding agentsKTPH026, where the badge and the notifications have their own toggles; the rules are JSON files you can override under KTPH000. See KTPH027Coding agentsKTPH028.

KTPH004Control API and KTPH000KTPH005 — korTTY can now open a local socket so a script or a coding agent on the same computer can list your windows, read any pane, type into it, wait for output, split a local shell, and drive a detected coding agent. It is KTPH006off by defaultKTPH007 and is switched on under KTPH008Settings → Terminal → Control APIKTPH009, where a status line reports what the listener is actually doing. Nothing is reachable over the network and no other user of the computer can connect: the endpoint lives in an owner-only KTPH001 directory and needs a token that is regenerated on every start. Every action is logged with byte counts only, never terminal text, and the first time a program types into a pane you get one desktop notification, so a takeover is never silent. An administrator can deny the feature outright with the KTPH002 policy key. The KTPH003 client ships beside the application in every native package and handles discovery, authentication and exit codes for you. See KTPH010Control APIKTPH011 and KTPH012Control CLIKTPH013.

KTPH000Command timestamps stay on their command linesKTPH001 — once the scrollback had reached its limit, the marks in the command timestamp sidebar drifted one row further from their command with every new line of output, and a new prompt on the bottom row got no mark of its own. Marks now move with their lines, disappear when their line leaves the scrollback, and are removed by KTPH002Clear BufferKTPH003. The dates in the sidebar and its hover popup follow the UI language instead of a fixed German order, and KTPH004DuplicateKTPH005 and KTPH006No GroupKTPH007 in the tab context menu are translated instead of always German. See KTPH008Terminal settingsKTPH009.

KTPH000Anonymous usage statistics now cover coding agents and the Control APIKTPH001 — if you allowed anonymous statistics, korTTY also reports which agent kinds are detected, how often agent notifications fire, which Control API methods are used and whether the coding-agent and Control API settings are on. Only kinds, states, method names and counts are sent — never terminal text, prompts or pane names. See KTPH002Anonymous dataKTPH003.

KTPH004Tabs that close on their own are fully releasedKTPH005 — when a split pane was left as the last pane and its shell exited, or KTPH006KTPH000KTPH007+KTPH008KTPH001KTPH009 closed a local cmd or PowerShell tab, the tab closed without the cleanup its close button runs: korTTY still counted that pane as connected, so with KTPH010Configuration KTPH016 Prevent System SleepKTPH011 checked the computer was kept awake, and a shell closed with KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015 kept running in the background. Such tabs now close exactly like a tab closed with its close button.

KTPH022Navigation keys reach programs the way they expect themKTPH023 — korTTY used to send the arrow keys, Tab, Home/End, Page Up/Down, Insert/Delete and the F-keys as fixed sequences without their modifiers, so KTPH024KTPH002KTPH025+KTPH026KTPH003KTPH027 and KTPH028KTPH004KTPH029+KTPH030KTPH005KTPH031 arrived as plain Left and Tab and KTPH032KTPH006KTPH033+KTPH034KTPH007KTPH035 as F1. They are now encoded the xterm way and follow the program's cursor-key mode, so word movement (KTPH036KTPH008KTPH037+KTPH038KTPH009KTPH039 / KTPH040KTPH010KTPH041+KTPH042KTPH011KTPH043, KTPH044KTPH012KTPH045+KTPH046KTPH013KTPH047 / KTPH048KTPH014KTPH049+KTPH050KTPH015KTPH051 on macOS) and back-tab work in the shell, KTPH000 and KTPH001. KTPH052KTPH016KTPH053+KTPH054KTPH017KTPH055 / KTPH056KTPH018KTPH057+KTPH058KTPH019KTPH059 now scroll korTTY's scrollback, KTPH060KTPH020KTPH061+KTPH062KTPH021KTPH063 switches tabs while the terminal has the focus, editing the find bar's search text no longer types into the shell, and broadcast mode mirrors these keys to every pane, encoded for each. See KTPH064Keyboard shortcutsKTPH065.

KTPH009Ctrl+L and Ctrl+F reach the shell on Windows and LinuxKTPH010 — the terminal's own Clear Buffer and Find took these keys, so KTPH011KTPH001KTPH012+KTPH013KTPH002KTPH014 wiped the scrollback instead of redrawing the screen in bash, psql or a REPL, and KTPH015KTPH003KTPH016+KTPH017KTPH004KTPH018 never moved the cursor forward or paged forward in KTPH000. Both keys now go to the shell; Clear Buffer and Find stay in the terminal's right-click menu and Find in KTPH019Edit → Find…KTPH020, while KTPH021KTPH005KTPH022+KTPH023KTPH006KTPH024 and KTPH025KTPH007KTPH026+KTPH027KTPH008KTPH028 on macOS are unchanged. On Linux a selection copied automatically also becomes the X11 primary selection, so a middle-click pastes it in other applications. See KTPH029Keyboard shortcutsKTPH030.

KTPH000The ANSI colors and the selection color on the Colors tab now take effectKTPH001 — the 16 color pickers in KTPH002Settings → ColorsKTPH003 were never saved, and the terminal ignored the KTPH004SelectionKTPH005 color too. Both now apply to every open terminal as soon as you save, and terminal recordings use the same colors as the screen. Settings you never changed keep the built-in palette and inverse-video selection, so nothing looks different until you customize a color. KTPH006Bold as bright colorKTPH007 still affects recordings only. See KTPH008ColorsKTPH009.

KTPH001Review and replace a changed host keyKTPH002 — when a server was rebuilt, the changed-key alert of a terminal tab or the SFTP manager now offers KTPH003Review and Replace…KTPH004: it shows the trusted and the new SHA-256 fingerprint side by side and replaces the key only after you tick that you verified the new fingerprint with the server administrator. KTPH005CloseKTPH006 and KTPH007CancelKTPH008 stay the default buttons, background connections never offer the replacement, and the KTPH000 policy forbids it. The new KTPH009Configuration → Security → Known Hosts…KTPH010 lists, searches and removes trusted keys. See KTPH011SSH host-key verificationKTPH012.

KTPH005SSH tunnels now really openKTPH006 — tunnels configured on a connection were saved, imported and shared, but never opened. korTTY now opens the enabled ones once per terminal tab after login, closes them before a reconnect and opens them again afterwards, moves them to another pane of the same server when you close the pane they run on, and shows KTPH000 with the first error in the tab's status bar (hover for every tunnel). Because tunnels that never did anything would otherwise start listening silently after the update, korTTY asks once per connection before it opens them, and again when the tunnels or the server change. A remote tunnel listens on the SSH server's loopback address unless you name another one, shared (Teamwork) connections never open remote tunnels and may only listen on KTPH001, and administrators can forbid tunnels with the new KTPH002 policy key. Remote tunnels that earlier versions imported from PuTTY Connection Manager carry the bind address KTPH003; the confirmation, the tunnel list and the status bar mark them as reachable from other computers, so set their KTPH007Remote bind addressKTPH008 to KTPH004 if the forwarded port should stay private to the server. See KTPH009SSH TunnelsKTPH010.

KTPH001The tunnel editor says what listens where, and Enable SSH tunnels worksKTPH002 — the tunnel dialog now labels its fields after their role for each type (KTPH003Local bind addressKTPH004, KTPH005Remote bind addressKTPH006, KTPH007Local hostKTPH008 as a remote tunnel's target), lists the listener first and warns when other computers can reach it; the tunnel list shows remote tunnels listener first instead of reversed and no longer shows German text for SOCKS proxies. KTPH009Enable SSH tunnelsKTPH010, which nothing ever read, now switches every tunnel of the connection on or off, and saving the connection applies tunnel changes to open tabs right away, so switching tunnels off closes them. KTPH011CancelKTPH012 now discards tunnels added, edited or removed in the connection editor, which were kept before. PuTTY Connection Manager imports bind remote tunnels to KTPH000. See KTPH013SSH TunnelsKTPH014.

KTPH005SSH tunnels now really openKTPH006 — tunnels configured on a connection were saved, imported and shared, but never opened. korTTY now opens the enabled ones once per terminal tab after login, closes them before a reconnect and opens them again afterwards, moves them to another pane of the same server when you close the pane they run on, and shows KTPH000 with the first error in the tab's status bar (hover for every tunnel). Because tunnels that never did anything would otherwise start listening silently after the update, korTTY asks once per connection before it opens them, and again when the tunnels or the server change. A remote tunnel listens on the SSH server's loopback address unless you name another one, shared (Teamwork) connections never open remote tunnels and may only listen on KTPH001, and administrators can forbid tunnels with the new KTPH002 policy key. Remote tunnels imported from PuTTY Connection Manager carry the bind address KTPH003; the confirmation and the status bar mark them as reachable from other computers, so set their KTPH007Remote hostKTPH008 to KTPH004 if the forwarded port should stay private to the server. See KTPH009SSH TunnelsKTPH010.

KTPH000The terminal encoding now takes effectKTPH001 — KTPH002Settings → Terminal → EncodingKTPH003 was never read, so every SSH session was decoded as UTF-8 and servers that write ISO-8859-1, ISO-8859-15 or Windows-1252 showed broken umlauts. The setting now applies to SSH connections, and each connection can choose its own KTPH004Character encodingKTPH005 on the KTPH006ConnectionKTPH007 tab of the connection editor. Local shells stay UTF-8 unless their connection sets an encoding, and Mosh is always UTF-8. A value you picked in an earlier version, when it had no effect, is not applied on its own: SSH sessions stay UTF-8 until you save the settings after opening the Terminal page, where a note points this out. Text that the KTPH008Control APIKTPH009 types into a pane follows the pane's encoding as well. See KTPH010Character encodingKTPH011.

KTPH000Temporary SSH keys are no longer left in the temp folderKTPH001 — every connect, split and SFTP session with a temporary SSH key wrote the private key to a file in the system temp folder that was never deleted, so the key stayed on disk long after it had expired, and the debug log recorded the beginning and end of the key text. Temporary keys are now read in memory only and never logged, and key files that earlier versions left behind are deleted at the next start when they belong to you. See KTPH002SecurityKTPH003.

KTPH001Scheduled jobs delete their temporary key fileKTPH002 — a JobScheduler job with a temporary SSH key still needs the key as a file for Rsync's external KTPH000; that file is now created owner-only from the start and deleted when the job ends or its connection fails, instead of staying in the temp folder.

KTPH005JMX monitoring shows the connections that are really openKTPH006 — the KTPH000 MBean always reported 0 active connections and no names, because it read a session list that nothing ever filled. KTPH001, KTPH002 and KTPH003 now list every live SSH and Mosh terminal connection (each split pane counts, local shells do not), and KTPH004, which was never measured, stays at 0 for existing JMX clients. See KTPH007Logging and diagnosticsKTPH008.

KTPH001Scheduled jobs keep temporary keys off the disk tooKTPH002 — a JobScheduler job with a temporary SSH key now authenticates in memory like a terminal tab. Only an Rsync job still needs the key as a file for its external KTPH000; that file is created owner-only from the start and deleted when the job ends or its connection fails, instead of staying in the temp folder.

KTPH000Go back to an older llama.cpp or MLX runtimeKTPH001 — when a new runtime release causes problems, KTPH002Other version…KTPH003 in the Runtimes table of KTPH004AI → AI Manager → Local ModelsKTPH005 lists every version the signed stable channel still offers for this computer and installs the one you choose through the same verification as an update. A version other than the newest stays KTPH006pinnedKTPH007, so update checks keep it until you pick the newest version again or choose KTPH008UnpinKTPH009; a pinned version the channel later withdraws is dropped automatically. See KTPH010RuntimesKTPH011.

KTPH000Both runtimes stay visible in the Runtimes tableKTPH001 — the table had a fixed height that fit two rows only at the default font, so with a larger UI font scale or an AtlantaFX design only llama.cpp was visible and MLX needed scrolling. The table now sizes itself to its rows and follows font-scale and design changes while the AI Manager is open.

KTPH000Being offline is no longer reported as a failed runtime updateKTPH001 — the startup check for the llama.cpp and MLX runtimes ran into an error with a stack trace whenever the computer had no network yet. An unreachable channel now ends in an KTPH002OfflineKTPH003 status and a single log line, installed runtimes stay usable, and an installation you start yourself still says why it did not happen.

KTPH000MLX runtime updates are published like llama.cpp onesKTPH001 — the MLX index is now read from the same immutable, versioned releases as the llama.cpp index instead of a release whose files were replaced on every update; builds fall back to the previous location until the first combined release exists.

KTPH000Attach the selected file to an AI requestKTPH001 — when the text you right-click in the terminal is a single file name, KTPH002AI → Summarize / Solve Problem / AskKTPH003 and KTPH004Ask Agent…KTPH005 offer to send that file's content along with the request, so the model can work with the file rather than only its name. The file is resolved against the pane's current directory (over SFTP in SSH tabs, from disk in local-shell tabs) and is attached only after korTTY has checked that it exists, is readable, is UTF-8 text and fits the profile's selection limit; a checkbox in the confirmation dialog lets you send the text alone. The attachment is shown above the chat, stays in context for follow-up prompts and is kept with a saved chat. A KTPH006FlowchartKTPH007 button beside it renders a Mermaid flowchart of the attached script in the chat. See KTPH008Attaching a selected file to the chatKTPH009.

KTPH004Secrets in terminal selections are masked before they reach the AIKTPH005 — KTPH006SummarizeKTPH007, KTPH008Solve ProblemKTPH009, KTPH010AskKTPH011 and KTPH012Ask Agent…KTPH013 used to send the selected text and an attached file exactly as they were, including a password or token that happened to be on screen. korTTY now replaces the connection's password, your organization's journal replacement rules and well-known formats (private-key blocks, AWS, GitHub, GitLab and Slack tokens, KTPH000 API keys, bearer tokens, JWTs, passwords in URLs, KTPH001 assignments) with KTPH002, and the preview or the status bar says how many it masked. Only integrated models are exempt; an endpoint on KTPH003 is masked too unless you mark it as a KTPH014Trusted local endpointKTPH015 in the profile, because it may forward to a cloud API. Masking is pattern-based and cannot catch every secret. See KTPH016Masking secrets before sendingKTPH017.

KTPH004The AI agent asks before it runs in a switched sessionKTPH005 — after KTPH000, KTPH001 or a nested KTPH002 in a terminal, the agent's commands would still run over the tab's original connection, as the user the tab was opened with, not as the user the prompt shows. AI Agent and AI Planning now warn first and name the KTPH003 (or "on this computer" in a local-shell tab) the commands will really run as; KTPH006CancelKTPH007 is the default. The check also covers rerunning a command with the activity panel's reload button and the execution of an accepted plan. See KTPH008Safety and failure handlingKTPH009.

KTPH000No internet mode for native Anthropic profilesKTPH001 — korTTY sends no web tools to the native Anthropic Messages API, so a mode such as KorTTY Tavily Tool had no effect there. For such profiles the KTPH002Internet accessKTPH003 dropdown is now locked to KTPH004DisabledKTPH005 with a hint explaining why. See KTPH006AI internet accessKTPH007.

KTPH004The AI agent asks before it runs in a switched sessionKTPH005 — after KTPH000, KTPH001 or a nested KTPH002 in a terminal, the agent's commands would still run over the tab's original connection, as the user the tab was opened with, not as the user the prompt shows. AI Agent and AI Planning now warn first and name the KTPH003 (or "on this computer" in a local-shell tab) the commands will really run as; KTPH006CancelKTPH007 is the default. The check also covers rerunning a command with the activity panel's reload button and the execution of an accepted plan. See KTPH008Safety and failure handlingKTPH009.

KTPH000No internet mode for native Anthropic profilesKTPH001 — korTTY sends no web tools to the native Anthropic Messages API, so a mode such as KorTTY Tavily Tool had no effect there. For such profiles the KTPH002Internet accessKTPH003 dropdown is now locked to KTPH004DisabledKTPH005 with a hint explaining why. See KTPH006AI internet accessKTPH007.

KTPH000See what AI costsKTPH001 — an AI profile can now carry a price per one million input and output tokens (KTPH002AI → AI Manager → ProfilesKTPH003, KTPH004Price per 1M tokensKTPH005). With a price, korTTY shows the money spent next to the quota bar ("≈ 3.42 € in this period"), on session journals and in the AI Swarm header; local models are marked as having no token costs. See KTPH006Token quota managementKTPH007.

KTPH000Session journals show their AI tokensKTPH001 — every AI call made for a journal (summaries, title, screenshot analysis, questions) is added to the journal: the journal page header shows the total and the journal manager has an KTPH002AI tokensKTPH003 column with a breakdown in its tooltip. See KTPH004AI token usage and costKTPH005.

KTPH000All AI calls count towards the profile quotaKTPH001 — session journal calls, every AI Swarm agent and the swarm's combined answer, and scheduled AI jobs were not added to the profile's token quota before; they now are, so the quota bar reflects what was really spent. The AI Swarm header also shows the total tokens of the whole run.

KTPH001Scheduled AI agent jobs no longer hide a number in their outputKTPH002 — the job's token count was treated like a secret, so every occurrence of that number in the job's output and journal was replaced by KTPH000. It is now booked against the profile quota instead.

KTPH000Session journal per runKTPH001 — a job can now record a full session journal for every run: one journal per target server with every command, its output, the job's summary and the outcome, which can be summarized by the AI, searched, exported and asked questions like an interactive journal. Per job you choose when the AI summarizes (every kept run, only failed runs, or never), whether successful runs are kept at all, when the journals are deleted automatically (after N days, on a date, or never), a maximum number of runs and disk space, whether a run identical to the previous one is discarded in favour of a reference, and which AI profile summarizes — a local profile keeps it free. Switching the journal or its AI summaries on first shows a warning with an estimate of the tokens and cost per run, day and month. The run history shows each run's journals with tokens and cost and opens them in the viewer; scheduled AI Swarm jobs record one journal per server as well. Administrators can forbid automation journals or cap their retention, disk space and number of runs. See KTPH002Session journal per runKTPH003.

KTPH001Screenshots of jobs from an invisible virtual terminalKTPH002 — COMMAND and snippet jobs with a session journal can run in a pseudo terminal that korTTY renders without any window: screenshots at an interval, when the screen changes and at the end land in the run's journal, and a runtime limit stops monitors such as KTPH000 with Ctrl+C. Progress bars and AI coding tools in non-interactive mode become visible without disturbing the terminals you are working in. See KTPH003Virtual terminal and screenshotsKTPH004.

KTPH000Session journal per swarm runKTPH001 — the KTPH002Session journalKTPH003 checkbox in the AI Swarm toolbar records one journal per server for every run: the agent's commands and output, its answer and the combined report, with the same settings as a job (⚙) and the same cost warning. The dashboard reports what was kept and what the journal summaries cost, and KTPH004OpenKTPH005 shows the journals. See KTPH006Session journal per runKTPH007.

KTPH000Journals grouped by job and swarm, with badgesKTPH001 — the journal manager now groups automation journals by their job or swarm and by run, with the totals of each group, a filter for interactive, JobScheduler, AI Swarm, failed or pinned journals, and badges for the source, outcome, AI mode, identical runs, pin and the time left until automatic deletion. See KTPH002Managing journalsKTPH003.

KTPH000Temporary SSH keys are no longer sent to the AI with a multi-server workflowKTPH001 — KTPH002Generate multi-server workflowKTPH003 sent the complete private key of a temporary SSH key to the AI provider. The request now only states that the server uses a temporary key. The path of a key file is still sent, so the script can use it. See KTPH004Generate multi-server workflowKTPH005.

KTPH003Server output can no longer start an AI agent runKTPH004 — korTTY reacted to an escape sequence (KTPH000) anywhere in the output of an SSH session, such as a file shown with KTPH001, a login banner or anything a compromised server sends. It opened the AI agent run dialog filled in with a prompt and inline options such as KTPH002 chosen by the server, or started the run right away when the per-run setup dialog was turned off, and the same sequence moved the working directory korTTY tracks for the session. korTTY now ignores these sequences, so an agent command in the terminal starts a run only when you type or paste it. Prompt detection through OSC 133 markers and directory tracking through the shell's OSC 7 reports are unchanged. See KTPH005Terminal agent shortcut commandsKTPH006.

KTPH000Unlock the vault after startupKTPH001 — with KTPH002Require master password on startupKTPH003 turned off, korTTY started with the vault locked and offered no way to enter the master password later. KTPH004Configuration → Security → Unlock Vault…KTPH005 now opens the vault mid-session, and the "vault locked" messages for saving keys and passwords, AI Swarm, guide questions and workflow scripts have an KTPH006Unlock Vault…KTPH007 button that continues the action once the vault is open. Temporary SSH keys that a locked start could not decrypt are restored on unlock instead of being lost on the next save. See KTPH008Unlocking the vault laterKTPH009.

KTPH000Password targets behind a password jump server now connectKTPH001 — the terminal handed the master password only to targets that log in with an SSH key, and the SFTP tab not even to a temporary key, so a password or keyboard-interactive target failed on the jump server's stored password with "vault is locked" although the vault was open — and korTTY kept repeating that failed attempt through the whole retry count. The jump password now works whatever the target's authentication. Failures that another attempt cannot fix — a jump password that is missing, locked in the vault or cannot be decrypted, an incomplete jump setup, a rejected jump-server host key, an SSH key file that is missing or cannot be read — are reported once and no longer retried or reconnected automatically, and with a locked vault korTTY no longer contacts the jump server at all. See KTPH002When the jump server cannot be usedKTPH003.

KTPH000Robust uploads, a responsive server list and ReconnectKTPH001 — uploading a folder that already existed on the server failed at once; it now merges into the remote folder, and uploads are streamed, so files larger than the available memory or 2 GB no longer fail. Remote folders load in the background behind a KTPH002Loading…KTPH003 indicator, and a folder that cannot be opened keeps the one you were in. A remote copy onto the item itself or into one of its own subfolders is now refused — copying a file to the folder it was in used to empty it. When the connection drops, the status bar shows KTPH004Disconnected fromKTPH005 KTPH006hostKTPH007 with KTPH008ReconnectKTPH009 instead of Upload, Download and Refresh silently doing nothing. KTPH010SizeKTPH011 now sorts by the real byte count, the permissions fields accept only three octal digits, the menu entry is documented as KTPH012Connections → SFTP-Client...KTPH013, and the German UI says KTPH014ServerKTPH015 instead of KTPH016FernbedienungKTPH017. See KTPH018SFTP file managerKTPH019.

KTPH000SFTP tabs come back with a project, at their foldersKTPH001 — a saved project referred to its SFTP Manager tabs by connection name while opening it looked them up by id, so with KTPH002Auto-ReconnectKTPH003 no SFTP tab was ever restored, and the saved folders were ignored as well. Tabs are now saved by connection id and reopen at the local and remote folders they showed; a project saved earlier still restores a tab whose connection name is unique. A remote folder that is gone opens the login directory with a note in the status bar. Remote image tabs are saved with the connection they were opened from instead of the first SFTP tab's, so with several SFTP tabs open they no longer reopen from the wrong server. Restored remote image tabs now also connect with a key from the SSH key manager or through a jump server with a stored password, and close their own connection when you close them. See KTPH004SFTP Manager tabsKTPH005.

KTPH008Rename, New Folder, drag and drop and wildcard search in the SFTP ManagerKTPH009 — the guide described all four, but the SFTP Manager tab had none of them, and its search treated KTPH000 as a plain character. Both panels now rename with KTPH010KTPH006KTPH011 or the context menu, create folders from a toolbar button or the context menu, and delete with KTPH012KTPH007KTPH013 after confirmation; a rename never replaces an existing entry. Drag local rows or files from the desktop onto the remote panel to upload them and remote rows onto the local panel to download them, also straight into a folder row; up to 20 files with 16 MB together can be dragged from the server to the desktop. The search understands KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003 and KTPH004 and keeps KTPH005 visible. See KTPH014File operationsKTPH015 and KTPH016SearchKTPH017.

KTPH000Dialogs open noticeably fasterKTPH001 — the WebKit engine is loaded in the background after start instead of on the first dialog that needs it, the AI Manager and the settings dialog build their tabs on first visit, a stored connection's secrets are no longer re-derived on every open, and the snippet editor keeps a ready editor in reserve. Measured on a development build, the first AI Manager open dropped from about 1.4 s to under 0.1 s and the settings dialog from about 350 ms to 45 ms. The spare editor can be switched off with KTPH002Keep a pre-warmed editor readyKTPH003. See KTPH004Snippet Editor settingsKTPH005.

KTPH000The built-in guide has a new look and a working offline searchKTPH001 — the guide now uses the Dracula theme, because the previous theme reaches end of life in November 2026. Search works without a network connection and suggests results as you type, and German pages now declare German as their language, so screen readers and hyphenation use the right one.

KTPH000Clearer coding-agents diagram and a wider guide search fieldKTPH001 — the diagram on the coding-agents page shows one short note per box and no longer routes a line through other boxes, and the search field in the guide header is wide enough for its German placeholder.

KTPH000Flow diagrams keep loops a model drew in the wrong shapeKTPH001 — when a model drew a loop's condition as a plain action with two exits, the repair cut the exit after the loop and the whole diagram was replaced by the local fallback. Such a loop head is now turned into the loop decision.

KTPH002Flow diagrams from Nemotron and gpt-oss are no longer thrown awayKTPH003 — a model that writes all branches of a decision in one chain through KTPH004StopKTPH005 (KTPH000), as Nvidia Nemotron does, now gets that chain read as the decision's next outcome instead of the diagram being rejected, and repeated lines no longer make a complete diagram look hollowed out. Rounded nodes such as KTPH001 are read as actions. When a diagram is still rejected — for example because a local model such as gpt-oss derailed into garbled output — korTTY asks once more, naming the reason, before it uses the local fallback.

KTPH000Snippet Manager: more columns, resizable and rememberedKTPH001 — the snippet table shows KTPH002LinesKTPH003 and KTPH004Last modifiedKTPH005, every column (including KTPH006UsedKTPH007, which was too narrow to read, and KTPH008TagsKTPH009) can be resized, and korTTY remembers the widths. KTPH010ExportKTPH011 now proposes plain text script files first. See KTPH012SnippetsKTPH013.

KTPH001Import single text files as snippetsKTPH002 — KTPH003ImportKTPH004 accepts plain text files such as KTPH000, several at once; each becomes a snippet named after the file, with the language taken from the file extension. Binary files are skipped. See KTPH005Importing text filesKTPH006.

KTPH000Import and export snippet variablesKTPH001 — the Variable Manager exports all or the selected variables as JSON, XML or YAML and imports them again, asking whether existing values are overwritten. Its windows are larger, and the add/edit dialog explains both fields. See KTPH002Variable ManagerKTPH003.

KTPH008One workspace for all snippetsKTPH009 — the Snippet Manager shows the library and the snippets you edit side by side: browse in a read-only preview tab, edit in one tab per snippet, find a snippet with quick open (KTPH010KTPH000KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH001KTPH013), hide the library with KTPH014KTPH002KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH003KTPH017, and save or close tabs with KTPH018KTPH004KTPH019+KTPH020KTPH005KTPH021 / KTPH022KTPH006KTPH023+KTPH024KTPH007KTPH025. The open tabs and the window's size and position come back the next time. See KTPH026The Snippet Manager workspaceKTPH027.

KTPH000Unsaved snippets are never lostKTPH001 — every way of closing, including closing a main-window tab, opening a project and quitting, asks about unsaved snippet edits, and an editor's unsaved form is kept as a draft that can be restored after a crash.

KTPH000The Full code analysis lives in the editor and is storedKTPH001 — the analysis is a side panel inside the snippet editor, stored with the snippet the moment it arrives and shown again without a new AI request. A history keeps several analyses per snippet (KTPH002Stored analyses per snippetKTPH003 in the Snippet Editor settings), with pinning, discarding, KTPH004VerifyKTPH005 after applying, KTPH006Review laterKTPH007, and an apply run that can be continued even after a restart. The library's new KTPH008AnalysisKTPH009 column and filter show which snippets have open findings, a stale analysis or a pending review. See KTPH010Full code analysisKTPH011.

KTPH000AI changes are reviewed inside the editorKTPH001 — improvements, security fixes, AI formatting and the analysis's apply result replace the editor area with a side-by-side review instead of a blocking dialog, so terminals and other editors stay usable.

KTPH001Stop and retry any snippet AI requestKTPH002 — every AI action in the snippet editor shows its running time with KTPH003■ StopKTPH004 (also KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006) and offers KTPH007↻ RetryKTPH008 after a stop or failure; a stopped request really ends on the provider side.

KTPH000Before/after analysis reportsKTPH001 — export the stored analysis as PDF, HTML, Markdown or JSON before or after applying, save the analysed or final script as plain text, and export the reports of several snippets at once as one file or a ZIP.

KTPH000More reliable flow diagrams, and a zoom windowKTPH001 — a diagram the model got wrong is requested once more — repaired with the exact error where it can be — a fallback diagram says why it was used, and a click on the analysis diagram opens it in its own zoomable window.
KTPH000Analyses are part of the backupKTPH001 — the configuration backup includes the stored snippet analyses, and an unreadable snippet file is moved aside instead of being overwritten.

KTPH000Snippet foldersKTPH001 — organise the library in nested folders shown in a tree above the table, drag snippets and folders to move them, and export a whole folder as a ZIP or a directory that keeps its structure. See KTPH002FoldersKTPH003.

KTPH000Executable flagKTPH001 — each snippet is exported and copied as an executable (755) or a plain (644) file; scripts with a known extension or a shebang are executable automatically, and the flag can be changed in the Exec column or the editor. See KTPH002Executable flagKTPH003.

KTPH000Copy snippets and folders into the terminal directoryKTPH001 — copy selected snippets or a whole folder tree as files into the current directory of an SSH session (over SFTP) or a local shell, with the right file modes and an overwrite/skip choice for existing files. See KTPH002Copying files to the terminal directoryKTPH003.

KTPH000Analyse a folder as one project, and modularizeKTPH001 — the Full code analysis can examine a folder of scripts together and report problems between files, and the new KTPH002Propose modularizationKTPH003 option lets the AI split a script into modules that become files in a folder. Results that change several files are reviewed in a window with one tab per file and a directory tree that can be shown or hidden. See KTPH004Analysing a folder as one projectKTPH005 and KTPH006ModularizationKTPH007.

KTPH009Shell expansions stay as written, and typed values are stored only on requestKTPH010 — only the built-in placeholders and the variables declared in the Variable Manager are replaced, so KTPH000, KTPH001 or KTPH002 reach the shell unchanged instead of being sent empty or asked for, KTPH003 writes a literal KTPH004, and KTPH005 places the caret when a snippet is inserted into an editor. Send to Terminal asks for a declared variable without a value instead of sending it empty, Send to Terminal with Parameters lists every declared variable pre-filled, and a value you type is kept only when you tick KTPH011RememberKTPH012. Scheduled and swarm script runs still refuse an undeclared KTPH006, and a KTPH007 inside a word such as KTPH008 no longer cuts a shell line short when a script is sent as a one-liner. See KTPH013Placeholder variablesKTPH014.

KTPH003Passwords from an external command work on Windows and no longer freeze korTTYKTPH004 — a credential that fetches its password from a command such as KTPH000, KTPH001 or KTPH002 now runs it in PowerShell on Windows (it always failed there) and on the host in the Flatpak package. The 10-second limit now really holds: a tool that waits for input, an unlock or Touch ID is stopped together with the processes it started and reported, where it could hang korTTY forever before, and the connection editor fetches the password in the background while the field shows KTPH005Retrieving password...KTPH006. See KTPH007Passwords from an external commandKTPH008.

KTPH004GPG backups can be restoredKTPH005 — a GPG backup was saved under the ZIP name KTPH000, so importing it asked for a ZIP password and failed, and even a renamed KTPH001 file could not be restored. GPG backups are now saved as KTPH002 and import without a ZIP password; korTTY reads the format from the file content, so GPG backups made by earlier versions under the KTPH003 name restore too. See KTPH006Importing a backupKTPH007.

KTPH002A failed backup no longer pushes out the last good oneKTPH003 — the new backup is written completely before the current one is rotated into KTPH000, rotated GPG backups keep their KTPH001 ending, two backups in the same second no longer overwrite each other, and KTPH004Maximum BackupsKTPH005 counts ZIP and GPG backups together. See KTPH006Backup retention and cleanupKTPH007.

KTPH000More of your configuration is backed upKTPH001 — custom terminal themes, credential environments, saved AI Swarm chats and MLX model registrations are now part of the backup, and after an import korTTY reloads them together with SSH keys, snippet variables and AI chats instead of overwriting the restored files with what it had loaded before. A backup with another master password makes korTTY quit after the import, so you unlock the restored data with that password on the next start.
KTPH001The backup dialogs show their numbersKTPH002 — the confirmation after creating or importing a backup showed KTPH000 instead of the file name, size and number of files.

KTPH000No more options that did nothingKTPH001 — the Video Manager no longer offers a KTPH002Default formatKTPH003: recordings were always written as korTTY replay files, and WebM or MKV videos come only from KTPH004ExportKTPH005. A setting saved with the old WebM value still loads. The KTPH006Read-onlyKTPH007 checkbox is gone from the teamwork source dialog as well, because korTTY never writes back to a teamwork source; a value stored earlier is kept. The KTPH008TeamworkKTPH009 page now describes the one-way sync as it works. See KTPH010Terminal recordingKTPH011.

KTPH003A crash or a damaged file no longer costs you your connectionsKTPH004 — connections, credentials, SSH and GPG keys, environments, themes, scheduled jobs and KTPH000 are now replaced atomically and flushed to the disk instead of being rewritten in place, and on macOS and Linux KTPH001 and the files holding secrets are made owner-only. A file korTTY cannot parse at startup is moved aside as KTPH002 and listed in a notice instead of being overwritten with an empty list, and a file it cannot read at all is left untouched for the session. See KTPH005Stored security dataKTPH006.

Only the current release is listed here, so the guide stays short in every language it is translated into. Every version is on the KTPH002GitHub releases pageKTPH003; the curated notes for earlier versions are kept in the repository, in KTPH000 and KTPH001.
